subtopic_detail: Recognising raised intracranial pressure in a child previously labelled as having migraine
stem:
A 9-year-old girl is brought to your general practice by her mother. Six weeks ago another doctor diagnosed migraine and advised paracetamol and a symptom diary, but her mother is not satisfied.

The diary shows that on most mornings she wakes around 5 am with a headache, vomits once, and then feels well enough to go to school. There is no aura, no photophobia and no family history of migraine. She has not missed school and her marks are unchanged.

Her mother has noticed over the past fortnight that the girl holds her head tilted towards the left shoulder while watching television, which is new. On examination she is alert and orientated, with normal power and reflexes in all four limbs and no sensory loss. Fundoscopy shows blurred disc margins in both eyes. Her gait is slightly wide based when asked to walk heel to toe.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Blurred optic disc margins bilaterally, persistent left head tilt, wide based tandem gait, normal power reflexes and sensation in all limbs
data_table.History: Headache on waking with a single vomit then improvement, no aura, no photophobia, no family history of migraine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start propranolol as migraine prophylaxis and review her symptom diary in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Prophylaxis treats a diagnosis that the absent aura, absent photophobia, absent family history and the new neurological signs all argue against, and it delays recognition of a mass lesion by another 6 weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Headache

options.text: Refer to ophthalmology for formal assessment of the optic discs within 2 weeks
options.rationale: Confirming papilloedema does not change the need for urgent intracranial imaging, and a 2-week wait is unacceptable when the combination of morning vomiting, head tilt and ataxia already points to a posterior fossa process. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Headache

options.text: Arrange a lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure and relieve her symptoms
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture in the presence of papilloedema from an unconfirmed cause risks fatal tonsillar herniation if a posterior fossa mass is present; imaging must come first. It would be the right test only once a mass and hydrocephalus have been excluded and idiopathic intracranial hypertension is the working diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Raised intracranial pressure)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Raised intracranial pressure

options.text: Arrange same day magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and discuss with neurosurgery
options.rationale: Headache on waking that is relieved by vomiting, a new head tilt and an ataxic tandem gait with bilateral papilloedema is the classic posterior fossa syndrome and requires same day imaging with neurosurgical involvement. Magnetic resonance imaging is preferred because it images the posterior fossa without the beam-hardening artefact that limits computed tomography there. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Headache
Cancer Australia: Signs and symptoms of brain cancer in children

options.text: Arrange a non-contrast computed tomography head scan within the next week
options.rationale: The timeframe is too slow for papilloedema with focal signs, and computed tomography is the weaker modality for the posterior fossa, although it remains the right first test when magnetic resonance imaging is not available quickly or the child is deteriorating. (Source: RCH CPG: Headache)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Headache

explanation.summary: Brain tumours are the commonest solid malignancy of childhood and the majority in this age group sit in the posterior fossa, where they obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and raise intracranial pressure. The diagnostic delay in Australian series is measured in months, most often because episodic headache with vomiting is attributed to migraine. Distinguishing features are headache that is present or worst on waking, vomiting that relieves the headache, and any new neurological sign. A persistent head tilt in a child is an ominous sign that may reflect a fourth nerve palsy or tonsillar herniation rather than a musculoskeletal problem. Papilloedema is a late sign, so its absence never excludes the diagnosis.
key_points: Morning headache relieved by vomiting, plus any new neurological sign, mandates urgent intracranial imaging
A new persistent head tilt in a child is a posterior fossa red flag, not torticollis
Magnetic resonance imaging is the preferred modality for the posterior fossa; computed tomography is the rapid substitute
Lumbar puncture before imaging in a child with papilloedema risks herniation
Absent papilloedema does not exclude a tumour, since it appears late in the course
explanation.pearls: Migraine essentially never begins with headaches that consistently wake a child before dawn; a fixed early morning pattern over more than 4 weeks should trigger imaging rather than prophylaxis.

sources.label: Cancer Australia: Signs and symptoms of brain cancer in children

subtopic_detail: Acting on a migration percentage threshold during cerebral palsy hip surveillance
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community child development clinic. A 6-year-old boy with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy, classified as Gross Motor Function Classification System level V, attends for his annual review with his mother.

He is fully dependent for transfers and uses a supportive seating system. He takes baclofen and had botulinum toxin injections to both adductors 18 months ago. His mother reports no change in his comfort, and he shows no distress on handling or during nappy changes.

On examination hip abduction is 30 degrees on the right and 45 degrees on the left, with no fixed flexion contracture. The annual anteroposterior pelvis radiograph performed last week is reported with a migration percentage of 42 per cent on the right and 18 per cent on the left, compared with 26 per cent and 16 per cent a year ago.

data_table.Examination: Hip abduction 30 degrees right and 45 degrees left, no fixed flexion contracture, no pain on handling
data_table.Imaging: Anteroposterior pelvis radiograph migration percentage 42 per cent right and 18 per cent left; previous year 26 per cent right and 16 per cent left
data_table.Medications: Baclofen; botulinum toxin to adductors 18 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the pelvis radiograph in 6 months and continue the current surveillance schedule
options.rationale: Six-monthly radiographs are the surveillance interval for a level V child whose migration percentage sits below 30 per cent; once the threshold is crossed, surveillance is no longer the answer and referral is. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for assessment for hip reconstructive surgery
options.rationale: A migration percentage above 30 per cent triggers orthopaedic referral under the Australian hip surveillance guidelines, and a value of 42 per cent rising 16 points in a year indicates progressive displacement that usually needs bony reconstruction rather than soft tissue measures alone. Absence of pain is expected at this stage and is not a reason to wait, because the aim of surveillance is to intervene before the hip becomes painful and dislocated. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy
RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy

options.text: Repeat botulinum toxin injections to both adductors and reassess him in 6 months
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin reduces adductor tone and may improve seating comfort, but it does not reverse established displacement and there is no evidence it prevents progression once the migration percentage exceeds 30 per cent. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Fit a night-time hip abduction brace and reassess him clinically in 6 months
options.rationale: Abduction bracing has not been shown to prevent progressive hip displacement in cerebral palsy and is frequently poorly tolerated; it is a comfort and positioning measure, not a structural one. (Source: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy)
source_refs: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

options.text: Increase the baclofen dose and arrange physiotherapy review of his standing programme
options.rationale: Higher baclofen doses reduce tone and may help care and comfort but do not alter the mechanical course of hip displacement, and a level V child has no independent standing programme to modify. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy

explanation.summary: Hip displacement affects around a third of children with cerebral palsy and the risk rises steeply with Gross Motor Function Classification System level, reaching about 90 per cent at level V. Australian hip surveillance programmes were built on this relationship: they set radiograph frequency by motor level and age, and use the migration percentage, the proportion of the femoral head lying lateral to Perkin's line, as the trigger for action. Referral is indicated at a migration percentage above 30 per cent or with progression of more than 10 percentage points per year. A dislocated hip in a non-ambulant child causes pain, difficulty with perineal care, seating problems and scoliosis, and salvage surgery at that stage is far less satisfactory than earlier reconstruction. Pain is a late and unreliable marker, which is exactly why radiographic surveillance exists.
key_points: Migration percentage above 30 per cent, or progression over 10 points in a year, triggers orthopaedic referral
Surveillance frequency is set by Gross Motor Function Classification System level; level V children need annual or six-monthly radiographs from 2 years of age
Absence of hip pain does not justify delay, since pain appears once displacement is advanced
Botulinum toxin, baclofen and bracing address tone and comfort but do not prevent progressive displacement
Late salvage surgery for a dislocated hip gives poorer outcomes than timely reconstruction
explanation.pearls: Migration percentage is measured from a standardised anteroposterior pelvis film with the legs in neutral rotation; a rotated film falsely alters the value, so check positioning before acting on a borderline reading around 30 per cent.

sources.label: Australian Hip Surveillance Guidelines for Children with Cerebral Palsy

subtopic_detail: Referred knee pain with obligate external rotation in an adolescent
stem:
You are the resident in a suburban emergency department. A 13-year-old boy attends with his mother because of 5 weeks of a dull ache in his left knee that is worse after sport. There was no injury and no swelling of the knee at any point.

He has walked with a limp for the last fortnight, which his football coach attributed to a muscle strain. He has had no fevers, sweats or weight loss, and he has been eating and sleeping normally. His body mass index is on the 97th centile for age.

On examination the left knee has full painless range of movement, no effusion, no joint line tenderness and stable ligaments. When you flex the left hip, the leg rolls into external rotation and he cannot keep it in neutral. Blood tests taken at triage show a C-reactive protein of 2 mg/L (less than 5) and a white cell count of 7.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 100% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Left knee full painless range with no effusion, obligate external rotation of the left leg on hip flexion, antalgic gait
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 7.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)
data_table.Growth: Body mass index on the 97th centile for age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an outpatient magnetic resonance imaging scan of the left knee within 2 weeks
options.rationale: The knee examination is entirely normal, so imaging it will be unrevealing; this is the referred-pain anti-pattern in which the symptomatic joint rather than the affected joint is investigated. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the left hip looking for a joint effusion, then review
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the right first test for suspected transient synovitis or septic arthritis in a younger child, but a normal C-reactive protein and afebrile state make infection unlikely and ultrasound cannot show the bony slip. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute limp

options.text: Refer him to physiotherapy for a graded quadriceps programme and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Treating this as a soft tissue overuse problem allows continued weight bearing, and further slip during that period converts a stable presentation into an unstable one with a markedly higher risk of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Take blood cultures and arrange an urgent hip aspiration under image guidance
options.rationale: Aspiration is the investigation for suspected septic arthritis, which a 5-week history, normal temperature, normal white cell count and normal C-reactive protein together make very unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute limp)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Acute limp

options.text: Make him non-weight-bearing and arrange urgent pelvis radiographs with orthopaedic referral
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion in an overweight adolescent with weeks of knee pain and a limp is the classic presentation of a slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and radiographs must include a frog-leg lateral because early slips are missed on the anteroposterior view alone. Immediate non-weight-bearing and orthopaedic referral prevent progression to an unstable slip. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
RCH CPG: Acute limp

explanation.summary: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis typically presents between 10 and 16 years, is more common in boys and strongly associated with obesity, and around a quarter of cases present with knee or thigh pain alone because of referral through the obturator nerve. Delay is the single biggest determinant of outcome: a stable slip, in which the child can still weight bear, has a low risk of avascular necrosis, whereas an unstable slip carries a risk in the order of 20 to 50 per cent. Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion is the most reliable bedside sign. Around 20 per cent of cases are bilateral at presentation and more become so later, so both hips are imaged and the contralateral hip is monitored. Endocrine screening is considered where the child is younger than 10, underweight or unusually short, since hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency and renal osteodystrophy are recognised associations.
key_points: Any adolescent with knee pain and a limp needs the hip examined and imaged
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the key bedside discriminator
Request anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvis views; early slips are invisible on the anteroposterior view alone
Make the child non-weight-bearing immediately, since progression to an unstable slip sharply raises the risk of avascular necrosis
Image both hips, as around 20 per cent are bilateral at presentation
explanation.pearls: On the anteroposterior film, draw Klein's line along the superior femoral neck: in a normal hip it intersects part of the femoral head, and failure to do so indicates a slip.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

subtopic_detail: Immediate airway and pouch management in a newborn who cannot pass a nasogastric tube
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the postnatal ward to see a term baby girl born 2 hours ago by normal vaginal delivery in a regional hospital with a level 2 nursery.

The midwife reports that the baby has needed suctioning four times for frothy bubbly secretions at the mouth, and coughed and went briefly dusky when offered her first breastfeed. The antenatal 20-week scan was reported as showing increased amniotic fluid and a stomach bubble that could not be visualised.

The baby is now pink in air with good tone and a normal cry. The midwife attempted to pass a size 8 French nasogastric tube, which met firm resistance at 11 cm from the gums and could not be advanced. The nearest paediatric surgical centre is a 2-hour road transfer away and the retrieval service has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Frothy oral secretions requiring repeated suction, good tone and cry, no respiratory distress at rest, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Antenatal history: Increased amniotic fluid on the 20-week scan with a non-visualised stomach bubble
data_table.Procedure: Size 8 French nasogastric tube meets resistance at 11 cm from the gums

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Pass a wide bore replogle tube on continuous low suction and keep the baby nil by mouth
options.rationale: A double lumen replogle tube on continuous low suction empties the blind upper pouch and is the single measure that prevents ongoing aspiration of pooled saliva during the hours before transfer and surgery. Keeping the baby nil by mouth and nursing head-up completes the holding management. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network clinical practice resources

options.text: Arrange a contrast swallow study to define the level of the obstruction before transfer
options.rationale: Contrast in a blind upper pouch spills into the airway and causes chemical pneumonitis; a plain chest and abdominal radiograph with a firm tube in situ answers the anatomical question safely. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

options.text: Intubate and ventilate the baby electively for the road transfer to the surgical centre
options.rationale: Positive pressure ventilation can preferentially inflate the stomach through a distal fistula, causing gastric distension, splinting of the diaphragm and even perforation; intubation is reserved for babies who genuinely need it for respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

options.text: Start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin for presumed early onset neonatal sepsis
options.rationale: The baby is afebrile with normal perfusion and the secretions have a mechanical explanation, so empirical sepsis therapy addresses the wrong problem; antibiotics may be started later if aspiration pneumonitis develops. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal sepsis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal sepsis

options.text: Nurse the baby flat and commence slow continuous nasogastric feeds until the retrieval team arrives
options.rationale: Feeding cannot be delivered through a tube that will not pass, and nursing flat increases the risk of reflux of gastric contents up through a distal fistula into the trachea. Head-up positioning is preferred. (Source: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula

explanation.summary: Oesophageal atresia occurs in about 1 in 3500 births and is frequently signalled antenatally by polyhydramnios with a small or absent stomach bubble, although these findings have low positive predictive value on their own. The postnatal hallmark is excessive frothy oral secretions with choking on the first feed, and the bedside test is the inability to pass a firm tube beyond about 10 cm. Holding management aims entirely at protecting the airway from two sources of soiling: saliva pooling in the blind upper pouch, and gastric acid refluxing up a distal fistula. Associated anomalies occur in around half of cases, so echocardiography, renal ultrasound and careful examination of the anus and limbs are performed before or soon after surgery. Definitive repair is undertaken at a paediatric surgical centre.
key_points: Frothy secretions with choking on the first feed plus a tube that will not pass beyond about 10 cm is the clinical diagnosis
A replogle tube on continuous low suction with head-up nursing and nil by mouth is the holding management
Contrast studies risk aspiration pneumonitis; a plain radiograph with the tube in situ is the safe confirmatory image
Avoid elective positive pressure ventilation where a distal fistula may be present, because of gastric distension
Screen for associated cardiac, renal, vertebral, anorectal and limb anomalies before repair
explanation.pearls: Gas in the stomach and bowel on the plain film means a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula is present, whereas a gasless abdomen indicates pure atresia and predicts a long gap needing delayed repair.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network clinical practice resources

subtopic_detail: First line genetic testing for global developmental delay with a suggestive maternal pedigree
stem:
A 4-year-old boy is referred to your developmental paediatrics clinic because he has no single words and does not point to share interest. He flaps both hands when excited and becomes distressed by the hand dryer in public toilets.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, with a normal newborn bloodspot screen and a normal newborn hearing screen. Formal audiology at age 3 confirmed normal hearing thresholds bilaterally.

His mother mentions that her brother lives in supported accommodation and has never worked because of an intellectual disability that was never explained. Her own mother stopped having periods at 38 and developed a tremor and unsteadiness in her early sixties that has been attributed to ageing.

On examination his head circumference is on the 90th centile, he has a long face with prominent ears, and his joints are hypermobile. He makes poor eye contact throughout the consultation.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference on the 90th centile, long face with prominent ears, generalised joint hypermobility, hand flapping, poor eye contact
data_table.Investigations: Normal newborn bloodspot screen; audiology at age 3 with normal thresholds bilaterally
data_table.Family history: Maternal uncle with unexplained intellectual disability; maternal grandmother with cessation of periods at 38 and a late-onset tremor with unsteadiness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial genetic investigation?

options.text: Standard karyotype with fluorescence in situ hybridisation for common microdeletions
options.rationale: Karyotype resolves only rearrangements larger than about 5 to 10 megabases and has been superseded as a first line test by microarray, which detects far smaller copy number changes across the whole genome. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental delay

options.text: Methylation studies of chromosome 15 for Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes
options.rationale: Targeted methylation testing is appropriate when the phenotype fits, which would require neonatal hypotonia and hyperphagia, or the ataxic gait with a happy demeanour and severe speech absence of Angelman syndrome; neither matches this boy. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental delay

options.text: Chromosomal microarray in parallel with FMR1 CGG trinucleotide repeat analysis
options.rationale: Australian practice pairs chromosomal microarray with FMR1 repeat analysis as the first line for unexplained global developmental delay, and the pedigree here of an affected maternal uncle, premature ovarian insufficiency in the grandmother and her late-onset tremor with ataxia is the recognisable X-linked signature of an expanding FMR1 repeat across generations. Microarray is still done in parallel because copy number variants remain the commonest single yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental delay
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice

options.text: MECP2 sequencing and deletion or duplication analysis for a Rett spectrum disorder
options.rationale: Classic Rett syndrome affects girls and features developmental regression with loss of purposeful hand use and acquired microcephaly, none of which fits a boy with a head circumference on the 90th centile. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental delay)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental delay

options.text: Whole exome sequencing of the child with both parents sequenced as a trio
options.rationale: Exome sequencing has a real place in Australian practice but sits at the second tier, undertaken through a clinical genetics service after microarray and FMR1 testing are non-diagnostic. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice

explanation.summary: Fragile X syndrome is the commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability and results from expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. Because a maternal premutation expands to a full mutation when transmitted, the family history often shows affected males in the maternal line alongside premutation carriers with their own distinct phenotypes. Two of those carrier phenotypes are diagnostically valuable: fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency in women, and fragile X-associated tremor and ataxia syndrome in older carriers of either sex. The physical features in the child, a long face, prominent ears, macrocephaly and joint hypermobility, are supportive but often subtle before puberty. A diagnosis has direct implications for reproductive counselling across the extended family, which is why cascade testing through a clinical genetics service follows confirmation.
key_points: Chromosomal microarray plus FMR1 repeat analysis is the first line pair for unexplained global developmental delay in Australia
Premature ovarian insufficiency and late-onset tremor with ataxia in the maternal line are premutation carrier signatures
Repeat expansion occurs on maternal transmission, so affected males cluster in the maternal line
Exome sequencing is a second tier test arranged through clinical genetics after first line testing is negative
A confirmed diagnosis triggers cascade testing and reproductive counselling for the wider family
explanation.pearls: FMR1 repeat sizes matter: under 45 is normal, 45 to 54 is intermediate, 55 to 200 is a premutation carrying ovarian insufficiency and tremor-ataxia risk, and over 200 is the full mutation causing fragile X syndrome.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Genomics in general practice
